fr.elements: Main Building; Front Driveway; Access Road; Landscaped Area; Open Green Space; Perimeter Fencing; Pedestrian Walkways; Street Frontage; Detached Structure; Open Terrain
fr.considerations: Single Access Point; Long Driveway; Dense Vegetation; Limited Rear Access; Open Terrain
fr.recommendations: Providing the property with a clearly marked, well-identified address visible from the access road could improve responder navigation, particularly given the single entry point and extended driveway approach. Ensuring the driveway width and overhead clearance along its full length would support apparatus movement and reduce delays during emergency operations. Where dense vegetation borders the driveway or walkways, maintaining adequate clearance along travel corridors may enhance responder movement toward both the main building and the detached structure. Given limited rear access, identifying and communicating any secondary pedestrian pathways to the rear of the property in advance could assist responders in establishing tactical positioning during an incident.

wildfire.conditions: Scattered Shrubs; Dense Shrub Cover; Continuous Shrub Cover; Brush Adjacent to Structure; Structure Surrounded by Vegetation; Irrigated Landscape; Limited Defensible Space; Wildland Interface; Fuel Continuity; Single Access Route; Vegetated Access Route; Open Terrain
wildfire.recommendations: Reducing brush immediately adjacent to the structure and creating greater separation between dense and continuous shrub cover and the building perimeter would improve defensible space and reduce fuel continuity near improvements. Where shrubs directly contact or closely border the structure, thinning and clearing that vegetation could meaningfully reduce direct flame and radiant heat exposure to the building. Managing vegetation along the single access route is particularly important, as maintaining adequate width, vertical clearance, and reduced fuel concentrations along this corridor would support firefighter access and safe evacuation. Given the property's wildland interface setting and open terrain, preserving and expanding any irrigated landscaping near the structure as a fuel break may further reduce opportunities for fire spread. A sustained vegetation management program addressing the surrounding shrub cover within the immediate structure zone would support long-term wildfire resilience and improve overall property preparedness.
